newsitem.title: JAPAN: Securities tax cut idea part of tax debate - MOF.
newsitem.headline: Securities tax cut idea part of tax debate - MOF.

text.p: The Finance Ministry regards the possible scrapping of taxes on securities transactions as something to be discussed as part of overall reform of Japan's tax system, a ministry official told Reuters on Thursday.
The reforms are planned for the year from April 1, 1998.

But the official said the tax issue must not be considered as a special measure to deal with the recently fragile Tokyo stock market. "The issue is one topic to be discussed under an overall tax reform for 1998/99. We do not regard it as a special measure we should discusss to deal with the recent plunge in stock prices," he said.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Wednesday that it is proper to discuss the issue of scrapping securities transactions taxes as a part of planned reforms of Japan's financial system and securities tax system.
Japanese media have reported that some senior members of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) are calling for the scrapping of the taxes to help push up stock prices.

The national daily Asahi Shimbun reported on Thursday that Taku Yamasaki, chairman of the LDP's policy-making committee, cancelled a plan on Wednesday to refer to specific stock measures in a speech delivered in parliament's Lower House.
The paper said that in his original speech Yamasaki had planned to call on Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to scrap taxes on securities transactions and to liberalise brokerage commissions.

He had also planned to urge a review of double-taxation on dividends, the removal of rules regulating management of corporate pension funds, simplification of procedures to allow companies to buy back their own shares, and the introduction of stock options, the paper said.
In the end Yamasaki merely asked Hashimoto what he planned to do about sagging stock prices and did not put forward specific proposals.
The paper said Yamasaki decided not to mention specific measures as Hashimoto, who also is the LDP president, has been cautious about taking any new measures to counter sluggish stock prices.
